questions.q: What does it mean for an automation script to be 'idempotent'?
options: The script can only be run exactly one time, ever
The script automatically deletes resources after use
The script runs faster each time it's executed
Running it once or running it five times leaves the infrastructure in the same end state, without duplicating resources or erroring
questions.explain: Idempotency means any number of runs converges on the same correct result, not that a script can only run once.

questions.q: Why does calling New-AzResourceGroup directly, with no check beforehand, fail on a script's second run?
options: PowerShell deletes resource groups automatically after each script run
The resource group already exists from the first run, and creating it again throws an error
New-AzResourceGroup can only be called once per PowerShell session
The second run always uses a different, invalid region
questions.explain: Without a check, the second run tries to create something that's already there, which errors out.

questions.q: What does Get-AzResourceGroup -Name "rg-prod" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue accomplish in the idempotent version of the script?
options: It forces the script to always create a new resource group
It checks whether the resource group already exists, without throwing an error if it doesn't
It permanently deletes the resource group named rg-prod
It renames the resource group to SilentlyContinue
questions.explain: This check lets the script test for existence safely, so it can decide whether to create the resource group or skip that step.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why do scripts get rerun more often than people expect?
options: PowerShell automatically reruns every script every 24 hours
A pipeline might retry a failed step, a teammate might reuse the script against a new environment, or someone reruns it after a small fix
Rerunning scripts is a feature unique to Azure Automation only
Scripts are never meant to be run more than once under any circumstance
questions.explain: Pipeline retries, reuse against new environments, and reruns after small edits are all realistic, common scenarios.

questions.q: What is the general 'check-then-act' pattern this lesson describes for idempotent scripts?
options: Verify whether a resource already exists in the desired state before deciding whether to create or change it
Delete the resource, then recreate it from scratch every time
Always create the resource first, then check if it worked
Only check resources that cost more than a certain dollar amount
questions.explain: The core idempotent pattern is checking a resource's current state first, then acting only if a change is actually needed.
